groundTruthNarrative: On 1 September four things changed at Harlow Bay at once. Tessaly Ground replaced Quillon as handler for both Corvane and Pelion. Corvane added two evening departures. Kiosk printer cleaning moved to fortnightly. And Corvane procurement switched every Harlow Bay counter and kiosk from Brackwater to cheaper Fennick tag stock. Corvane's departing mishandling rate rose from 4.1 to 7.6–7.9 per 1,000 passengers, and management blamed Tessaly's inexperienced crews. In fact, Fennick-printed tags fail automatic reading at about 12%, against about 1.5% for every other tag passing through the same arrays. When counters briefly went back to Brackwater stock (14–16 Oct), their no-read rate fell to 1.6% while kiosks still on Fennick stayed at 12%. The roughly six-fold rise in bags diverted to the unchanged two-person manual encode desk stretched evening dwell to about half an hour. Encode-path bags therefore reached laterals after closure and missed their flights. Corvane's auto-read bags showed no rise, and neither did Pelion's bags, which are worked by the same Tessaly crew pool. It is still unresolved whether Fennick stock is defective or simply needs different printer heat settings. The right step is to go back to Brackwater stock now. Penalising Tessaly would punish the wrong party.

answers.rationale: The initial file fits H1 well: the timing matches, 41% of staff are new, and both the manager and the VP blame the handler. C4 refutes it. Pelion moved to Tessaly on the same date, is worked by the same single crew pool, and its rate stayed flat (3.6–3.8). Corvane's auto-read bags, which crews load the same way, also stayed flat (3.9→3.7). The whole excess sits in encode-path bags, and 91% of those reached the lateral after its scheduled closing time, so they arrived too late for any crew to load them.

C9 shows the no-read rise is confined to Fennick-stock tags (11.8%), across both counters and kiosks. Other tags on the same arrays read normally, and the 14–16 Oct reversion to Brackwater brought counter tags back to 1.6%. C4 shows the resulting six-fold increase in encode-diverted bags, longer dwell, and encode-path bags arriving after lateral closure, while auto-read bags were unaffected. Together they establish the full chain. Neither item alone does: C4 cannot say why no-reads rose, and C9 cannot say that no-reads explain the missed flights.

If schedule compression were the cause, it would hit all evening bags, including auto-read ones. C4 shows Corvane's auto-read mishandling flat. The rise is confined to encode-path bags, whose volume rose from 70 to 455–470 a day while passengers fell, which two extra departures cannot explain. Check-in timing of encode-path bags matches auto-read bags.

C5's array repairs in September invite this explanation. But C9 shows transfer and Pelion tags reading at 1.3–1.4% within 0.3 points on every array, including array 3 before and after realignment, and Brackwater-stock tags read normally in October. Failing scanners would affect all tags.

Printer configuration was unchanged (E5), and Fennick stock fails on the same printers where Brackwater stock works (C9). That fits either a stock defect or a stock that needs higher printer heat. C9's engineer says the images cannot tell which. C7 (the supplier's own certificate, an interested source) and C8 (generic guidance) do not test the question. The claim is live but not established.

The evidence counts against the link itself. The same handler changeover, on the same date and with the same crews, left Pelion's rate flat and Corvane's auto-read rate flat. The excess bags missed flights because they reached the lateral after closure, which is not a crew loading failure. The C11 cause codes favouring 'failure to load' are assigned before tracing and are rarely checked against the definition.

Temporal order (switch on 1 Sep), specificity (only Fennick-range tags, at both counters and kiosks), the main rivals ruled out (same arrays read other tags normally; counters were not on the kiosk cleaning change) and a reversal (Brackwater at counters 14–16 Oct gave 1.6% while Fennick kiosks gave 12.1%) together establish causation.

Encode-diverted volume rose about six-fold, evening dwell rose from 7 to about 30 minutes, and 91% of the missed encode-path bags reached the lateral after scheduled closing. The encode-path mishandling rate rose from 0.2 to 3.8–4.2 while auto-read stayed flat. Check-in timing matches across paths, which rules out late check-in as a confounder.

Jam tickets rose from the same week the stock changed, so the two are associated. But kiosk preventive cleaning was halved on the same date, tickets are not split between kiosks and counters, and C14 records no cause for most callouts and no stock type. Causation is not established.

With H1 contradicted, a breach notice and fee withholding punish a handler whose crews are not causing the rise. It also starts a cure and retender process (C13) and leaves the tag problem untouched. It is damaging under H2 whichever way H5 turns out.

The October reversion showed Brackwater stock reads normally on the current printers. About five weeks of stock is in stores and the contract runs to 31 Dec (E5). Switching back removes the excess no-reads at source whether or not Fennick stock is defective, and it is easily reversed.

A defect claim would be justified if H5 were confirmed. But the evidence cannot yet separate defective stock from a printer-heat mismatch. If H5 is wrong, the claim is simply rejected and nothing lasting is lost.

Extra encode capacity would shorten evening dwell and reduce misses, so it is reasonable. But it treats the symptom, needs HBAA's cooperation, and becomes unnecessary once the stock is switched back. That makes it reasonable, not best.

With C4 and C9, the chain from Fennick stock to no-reads to encode backlog to missed flights is established, including a natural experiment. That is enough to commit to switching back to Brackwater stock. The open question in H5 does not affect that decision.

authoringNotes: Trap: everything changed on 1 Sep, and leadership claims only the handler changed (E6). E4 and E5 quietly contradict that, which keeps the case fair. C4 is the contrast case: Pelion, with the same handler, crews and date, stayed flat, and Corvane's auto-read path stayed flat. Only C4 settles H1, H3, R1, R3 and A1. C9 is the only item that ties no-reads to the tag stock, rules out the scanners and includes a reversal; it settles R2 and H4. Neither item alone supports H2. Distractors: C5 (array repairs, a lure towards H4), C11 (pre-trace cause codes favouring 'failure to load'), C10 and C3 (mixed staff and handler accounts), C16 (Tessaly's own figures elsewhere), C7 and C8 (interested or generic vendor material that leaves H5 open), C12 (encode staffing, relevant to A4 only), C14 (does not resolve R4). Reviewer checks: H5 stays unknown because no catalogue item independently tests the stock at adjusted heat settings. R4 stays association-only because the cleaning change has the same date and the tickets are not split between kiosks and counters. A4 is not preferred because switching the stock back removes the backlog at source within days. No action other than A2 is keyed preferred. All numbers reconcile: E1 and C4 match, and C4's routing split sums to the totals.
